analysis.one_liner: Makes oil companies pay the full cost of offshore oil spills instead of a capped amount.
analysis.headline: The bill to remove the $75 million cap on oil companies' spill liability never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, a company responsible for an oil spill from an offshore facility pays all cleanup costs plus up to $75 million in other damages, with taxpayers and the public left to absorb costs beyond that cap. S. 828 would have removed the cap entirely, making the responsible company liable for the full cost of every spill. The bill was introduced by Senator Menendez with five Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishermen, and taxpayers who currently absorb spill damages above the $75 million cap; the bill would make oil companies bear the full cost of the spills they cause.

how_it_helps.text: It strikes the $75 million liability limit in the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, so the responsible party must pay the full measure of damages under the Act for each spill from an offshore facility (other than a deepwater port).
It applies to oil discharged from offshore facilities into navigable waters or adjoining shorelines, covering cleanup costs and damages.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would face unlimited liability for spill damages instead of the current $75 million cap.

drawbacks.text: Removing the $75 million cap means potentially unlimited liability, which critics of such proposals have argued could deter offshore drilling or make it more expensive, with costs possibly passed to consumers at the pump.
The bill addresses only offshore facility liability under the Oil Pollution Act; it does not change other avenues of public exposure to oil spill costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is that taxpayers would no longer be on the hook for most spill damages from offshore oil; the main cost is that unlimited liability could make some smaller offshore operators uninsurable or push drilling activity to companies better able to absorb risk, and higher costs could be passed to consumers. Supporters judged the spill-payer guarantee worth those tradeoffs; the bill never received enough committee attention for that debate to play out.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Introduced April 25, 2013 by Senator Menendez with five Democratic cosponsors, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill's single substantive provision would have struck '$75,000,000' from the Oil Pollution Act and replaced it with full liability under section 1002.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil companies keep their $75 million liability cap, and taxpayers continue to absorb spill costs beyond that limit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil companies keeping the liability cap

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Bill Nelson, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, and Sheldon Whitehouse

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 25, 2013 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-led committee never took the bill up, so it was a one-party effort that died quietly.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their $75 million liability shield, making them pay the full cleanup and damage costs of spills. The bill's death preserves that cap.
Taxpayers currently absorb spill damages above the cap; the bill would have shifted those costs back to the companies. Its death keeps that exposure in place.
